stops.accessibility: Flat stone bridge with steps at both ends and no ramps. The lakeside paths are level but crowded at weekends.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open lakeside, no ticket and no gate.
stops.insiderTip: Stand mid-bridge at dusk and look west: the sun drops straight down the lake's axis, and the far shore's rooftops and willows line up like a cut-paper silhouette.
stops.name: Silver Ingot Bridge
stops.narration:
Stop mid-bridge and look down at the water on both sides. You are standing on the narrow waist between two lakes: Qianhai, the front lake, behind you, and Houhai, the rear lake, ahead. This pinch of stone is the Silver Ingot Bridge, named for its humped profile, which reminded someone of a yuanbao — the boat-shaped silver ingot, a lump of silver currency, that old China used as money.

The bridge is Ming dynasty stone, but the lakes are the real story. They are all that remains of a much bigger Yuan-dynasty water system: when Kublai Khan, the Mongol emperor who made Beijing his capital in the 1200s, built his palace city, engineers dug and linked lakes to float grain barges right up to the palace's back door. The capital ate because water carried its food. The barges are gone, but the shoreline pleasure trade stayed: teahouses, wine shops and lotus ponds that made this waterfront the city's evening quarter for centuries.

Turn slowly and read the rooftops. Grey tiles, low slopes, whitewashed gables — that is the hutong shoreline, lanes of courtyard houses pressing right to the water. A hutong is a narrow lane, and the word itself is Mongolian, left over from Kublai Khan's grid. The houses are siheyuan — courtyard compounds where rooms on four sides face inward onto one shared yard, the whole family's life turned toward the sky in the middle. People still live in these: laundry lines, birdcages, electric scooters wedged into alleys built for carts.

No ticket here, just wind off the water. Cross the bridge heading north, then turn right into the short slanted lane of shops. That is your next stop.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross the bridge heading north, then turn right into the short bustling lane angling north east — Yandai Xiejie, about 160 metres, roughly 3 minutes on foot.
stops.openingHours: Open lakeside, always accessible. Come in daylight for the views.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: MarcBogonovich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Paved but uneven flagstones, narrow in places, dense weekend crowds that barely leave room for wheels. Step-free at street level throughout.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the old chimney stacks shaped like tiny pagodas on the rooftops: they are the one Ming-era detail the souvenir shops never managed to cover up.
stops.name: Yandai Xiejie
stops.narration:
You have walked into a street shaped like a smoking pipe — or rather, named for one. Yandai means tobacco pipe, and xiejie means slanted street: this lane angles diagonally off the old grid because it once bent around the palace shoreline, and in the Qing dynasty, the Manchu emperors' era from the 1600s to 1912, it filled with pipe shops serving the bannermen and officials strolling the lakes. One of Beijing's oldest commercial streets, it has been selling things for the better part of eight centuries.

Here is the mechanism worth noticing: the shops are the old courtyard houses wearing new faces. Behind every glass front selling fridge magnets, a siheyuan — a four-sided courtyard compound — still stands, its rooms rented to shopkeepers, its back yard to families. That is the hutong economy in miniature. Tourism money pays the rents that keep the buildings standing, and the same money prices out the residents who gave the lanes their life: the guitar shop's upper floor may hold a family that has lived here since the 1950s, or an empty speculation flat. Supporters call this renewal; critics call it a stage set. Walk slowly and you will see evidence for both in a single block.

Buy nothing yet — the day's shopping comes later. Walk the lane's full short length, then head east toward the long north-south artery of Nanluogu Lane, about 960 metres, roughly 15 minutes through the hutongs.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk the lane to its east end, then head east through the hutong lanes toward Nanluogu Lane — about 960 metres, roughly 15 minutes on foot. Follow the lane signs; the Drum Tower's silhouette is your compass to the east.
stops.openingHours: Public lane, always open. Shops typically 10:00 to 21:00.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: wanghongliu, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Flat and paved, but extremely crowded on weekends — wheelchair users should come on a weekday morning. Side alleys are narrow with high kerbs.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public lane, no ticket. Courtyard-house museums along the lane may charge small separate fees; verify locally.
stops.insiderTip: Duck into any open side alley for thirty metres: the crowds vanish, the souvenir noise stops, and you see the working lane — coal piles, shared taps, neighbours playing chess.
stops.name: Nanluoguxiang
stops.narration:
This is the lane that made hutongs famous, and the first thing to know is that its fame nearly killed it. Nanluoguxiang — south gong lane, named for a lane shape someone thought looked like a gong mallet — runs under a kilometre north to south, laid out in the Yuan dynasty of the 1200s, and in the Ming and Qing centuries it housed Manchu banner families, the hereditary military households of the conquest elite, in grand courtyards with carved gate screens.

Then came the twentieth century's two truths. After 1949 the grand compounds were subdivided: one prince's courtyard became twelve families sharing one tap and one public toilet, which is why the lanes feel so lived-in — they were, densely, by people with no choice. Then, from the 1990s, demolition crews flattened whole hutong districts for towers and ring roads, displacing hundreds of thousands; this lane survived partly because it was rebranded early as heritage, its courtyards converted to cafes, hostels and boutiques. Supporters call that rescue; critics note the original residents mostly left and the lane became a mall in courtyard drag. Both things are true, and the side alleys prove it: step off the main drag and the commerce falls away into real lanes with real neighbours.

Walk the lane's length heading north. At its northern end the grey mass rising over the rooftops is the Drum Tower, about 990 metres, roughly 15 minutes on foot.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the lane to its northern end, then continue north toward the Drum Tower rising over the rooftops — about 990 metres, roughly 15 minutes on foot.
stops.openingHours: Public lane, always open. Shops typically 10:00 to 22:00; side alleys are residential, so keep voices down.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Anagoria, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Steep interior staircases to the upper floors with no lift. The courtyard and lake-facing views at ground level are step-free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed monument: about CNY 15 to 20 per tower at last check. Verify prices at the gate; Beijing monument pricing changes.
stops.insiderTip: Time your visit for one of the daytime drumming performances: two dozen drummers striking together is the only way to grasp how loud — and how far — the night watches carried.
stops.name: Beijing Drum Tower
stops.narration:
Look up: over forty metres of Ming-dynasty timber and brick, and for six centuries this was Beijing's alarm clock. The Drum Tower — Gulou — was first raised in 1272 under Kublai Khan, the Mongol emperor who founded this capital, and rebuilt in 1420 under Yongle, the Ming emperor who moved China's capital here from Nanjing. Inside it hung a hall of great drums, and every night the drummers beat the geng — the five two-hour watches into which old China divided the night — so that the whole northern city knew when the gates shut, when the patrols changed, and when dawn was coming.

The trick is the pairing. The old saying runs 'morning bell, evening drum': at dusk these drums sounded and the city's gates closed; at dawn the bell in the sister tower behind you rang and Beijing woke. Two buildings, one mechanism — sound as infrastructure, the way a siren or a phone network is today. What you hear now are replicas beaten in daytime performances, but stand under the eaves when two dozen drums strike at once and you will feel the original logic in your ribs.

Climb if your knees agree — the stairs are steep — for the rooftop view over the grey-tile sea of hutongs. Then walk about 140 metres north across the square to the smaller brick tower. That is the Bell Tower.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the north door and walk about 140 metres north across the square to the brick Bell Tower — roughly 3 minutes on foot.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 09:00 to 17:00 daily, last entry around 16:00. Verify locally as hours shift by season.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gisling, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Steep stairs to the bell chamber with no lift; the small square around the tower is level and step-free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed monument: about CNY 15 to 20 per tower at last check. Verify prices at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Ask the attendant to point out the bell's inscription band: the casting inscription names the Ming emperor Yongle's reign, which dates the bronze to 1420.
stops.name: Beijing Bell Tower
stops.narration:
The smaller tower holds the bigger voice. The Bell Tower — Zhonglou — is Qing dynasty brick, rebuilt in the 1700s after fire took its Ming predecessor, but the bronze hanging inside is older than the building by three centuries: cast in 1420 under the Ming emperor Yongle, some seven metres tall and weighing over sixty tonnes, one of the largest old bells in China.

Its job was the dawn half of the city's soundscape. Where the drums behind you counted out the night in two-hour watches, this bell rang the morning — gates opening, markets stirring, officials heading to court. And once a year it still speaks the old language: on lunar New Year the bell is struck 108 times, one stroke for each of the 108 afflictions — greed, anger, ignorance and their hundred-odd cousins — that Buddhism says cloud the human mind. Count them off and each ring is supposed to loosen one knot. The number is the teaching.

From here the walk changes key: temples instead of lanes. Head east toward the Confucius Temple and Imperial Academy — about 2.2 km, roughly 30 minutes on foot through the eastern hutongs. It is the longest leg of the day, flat and full of interest, so take it slowly.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head east from the square through the hutong lanes toward Guozijian Street and the Confucius Temple — about 2.2 km, roughly 30 minutes on foot. The route is flat; follow Andingmen Inner Street east, then turn south into Guozijian Street.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 09:00 to 17:00 daily, last entry around 16:00. Verify locally as hours shift by season.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Roman Boed, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Mostly level courtyards with some thresholds and steps into halls. The stone stelae forest is viewable step-free from paved paths.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Combined ticket with the Imperial Academy: about CNY 30 at last check. Verify prices at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Find the stelae carved with the names of top exam graduates: for centuries, newly passed scholars came here to read their own names in stone — the original honours board.
stops.name: Beijing Confucius Temple
stops.narration:
Step through the gate and the noise of the street falls away into cypress shade. This is the Kong Miao, Beijing's Temple of Confucius, raised in 1302 and second in scale only to the sage's own hometown temple. Confucius — Kongzi, the teacher of the 500s BC whose sayings on duty, study and filial respect shaped Chinese government for two thousand years — is honoured here not as a god but as the patron of learning itself.

Walk into the forest of stone tablets and you meet the machine that ran imperial China. Row upon row of stelae carry the names of more than fifty thousand jinshi — the advanced scholars who passed the highest level of the keju, the civil-service examinations, the gruelling multi-day essay ordeal by which peasant sons could, in theory, become ministers. It was the world's first large-scale meritocracy and also a cage: generations memorized the classics to climb it, and the state got loyal officials in return. Next door stands the Guozijian, the Imperial Academy founded in 1287, the empire's highest school, where the emperor himself sometimes lectured. Scholarship was the state religion here, exam success its heaven.

Photograph the courtyards and the old cypresses freely, but keep voices low — students still come to pray for exam luck. Then walk one block east to the yellow-tiled roofs. That is the Lama Temple.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the east gate onto Guozijian Street and walk one block east to the yellow-tiled roofs of the Lama Temple — about 980 metres, roughly 15 minutes on foot.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 08:30 to 17:00 daily; sometimes closed on Mondays. Verify locally before visiting.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Miguel Discart & Kiri Karma, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Level courtyards linked by thresholds and a few steps; very crowded, with jostling at hall entrances. Not step-free throughout.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed monastery: about CNY 25 at last check. A bundle of free incense sticks is handed out at entry. Verify prices at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the eaves as you walk the courtyards: the yellow glazed tiles mark imperial rank — only buildings with palace connections were allowed them.
stops.name: Lama Temple (Yonghegong)
stops.narration:
You smell it before you see it: sandalwood smoke hanging over five courtyards in a row. This is Yonghegong, the Lama Temple — lama meaning a Tibetan Buddhist teacher — and it began as a prince's mansion in 1694 before the Qianlong emperor converted it in 1744 into a monastery of the Gelug school, the reform order founded in the 1400s by the teacher Tsongkhapa, whose monks wear the yellow hats you will see everywhere here.

Take your free bundle of joss sticks — thin incense sticks burned as offerings, the smoke carrying prayers upward — and join the slow procession of the faithful: many are Han Chinese office workers, not Tibetans, because Tibetan Buddhism's blend of chanting, vivid imagery and formidable compassion has drawn millions of mainland followers. Walk the halls in order and the teaching builds: guardian kings, then the founders, then the Buddhas of past, present and future. Last stands the famous Maitreya — the future Buddha, the bodhisattva, an enlightened being who vows to stay in the world to help others, expected at the end of this age — carved from a single block of white sandalwood, eighteen metres above the floor and more below it. One tree, one guardian of tomorrow.

Two rules close the day. The courtyards and yellow roofs may be photographed; inside the halls, no photography, and never a close-up of a monk — worship is not a show. And if the incense smoke catches your chest, step upwind to the courtyard edges; November air already asks enough of your lungs.

This is the end of the walk. Retrace to the temple gate: the metro station outside connects across the city, and somewhere nearby a Peking duck — the lacquered roast duck first served to emperors and now to everyone — is waiting for your evening. You have earned it.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. The Yonghegong Lama Temple metro station (Lines 2 and 5) sits just outside the temple gate for connections across the city; the hutong lanes around Guozijian Street hold dinner options, including Peking duck restaurants, for the evening.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 09:00 to 16:30 daily, last entry around 16:00. Verify locally as hours shift by season.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 09:00 from October to November, when Beijing is crisp and the lakes are clear. Winter mornings bite below freezing, so layer up; summer brings crowds and sudden downpours instead.
tour.difficulty: Easy. About 5.4 km of flat walking, some 77 minutes on foot in total; steep stairs inside the two towers, thresholds and crowds at the temples.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.
tour.overviewText:
Step off a narrow stone bridge between two grey lakes on a cold November morning, an old man cycling past with a dog in his basket, and you are standing inside Beijing's oldest living rooms. This walk is your way through them.

A hutong is a narrow lane — the word itself is Mongolian, left from the 1200s when Kublai Khan laid out his capital in a grid — and its houses are siheyuan, courtyard compounds where rooms on four sides face inward onto one shared yard, a whole family's life turned toward the sky in the middle. Ordinary Beijingers still live in these lanes today: retired factory workers, migrant renters, a few wealthy restorers behind freshly painted gates, breakfast smoke mixing with cafe coffee. Whole districts were flattened in the 1990s and 2000s for towers and ring roads, and the argument follows you down every lane: supporters call the rebuilding renewal that gave families plumbing and sunlight, while critics mourn the courtyard homes and neighbourly bonds the bulldozers took, and both can point to streets that prove them right. Faith shares this ground too. A few streets apart stand a Confucian temple honouring scholarship and a monastery of the Gelug school — the Tibetan Buddhist reform order founded in the 1400s by the teacher Tsongkhapa, whose monks wear yellow hats — neighbours for centuries, neither having moved.

The walk starts at the water between the Qianhai and Houhai lakes, threads one old shopping lane and the long north-south current of Nanluoguxiang, climbs the city's two timekeeping towers, then heads east to the temples where the day dissolves into incense smoke.

November in Beijing is genuinely cold, often single digits Celsius, so wear layers and a windproof jacket; the lanes offer little shelter. Money is the yuan, marked ¥ or CNY — RMB, short for people's money, is its official name — and temple and tower tickets run about twenty to thirty yuan each, so carry small cash alongside your phone payment, verifying every price at the gate. At the Lama Temple, bundles of joss sticks — thin incense sticks burned as offerings — fill the courtyards with sweet smoke; if it catches your chest, stand upwind at the courtyard edges. One respectful rule covers both temples: photograph courtyards and roofs freely, never the inside of a worship hall, and never a monk close-up.

Come curious and unhurried. The lanes reward dawdlers, and somewhere near the end a roast duck is waiting.
tour.summary: A slow hutong day from the Shichahai lakes to the Lama Temple: old lanes, the Drum and Bell Towers, a Confucian temple and a Tibetan Buddhist monastery, all on foot.
tour.title: Hutongs, Towers & Lama Temple
